entry.title: Sports drinks
entry.question: What should you buy instead of a sports drink?
entry.decision: Plain coconut water, or plain water, nothing added.
entry.why: Coconut water carries potassium, sodium and magnesium, and in most cases regular water hydrates just as well.
entry.short_answer: Coconut water is the clear liquid inside green coconuts and carries potassium, sodium, magnesium and phosphorus. There is no proof it hydrates better than regular water. Sports drinks add the sweeteners, flavors, citric acid and added minerals traditional guides skip.
entry.detail: Coconut water is the clear liquid found inside green, unripe coconuts. It carries potassium, sodium, magnesium and phosphorus, the electrolytes, which can help replace what is lost to workouts, mild illness or heat; mineral amounts vary with the coconut’s maturity and some brands add sugar. Extension advice is that a healthy diet and regular water work just as well for most hydration. Traditional guides list drinks with high fructose corn syrup, artificial sweeteners, natural flavors, citric acid and added vitamins or minerals among drinks to avoid.

sources.name: Weston A. Price Foundation: Shopping guide categories

entry.kristy_take: Water does the hydrating. Coconut water is the plain swap when a sweeter drink is wanted.
buying_tips: Coconut water with only coconut water on the list.
Plain mineral water in glass or cans.
A list with no added sugar, natural flavors or citric acid.
watch_out: Added vitamins and minerals, artificial sweeteners and natural flavors sit on the traditional avoid list.
On blood pressure medication? Check the label minerals with a doctor first.
pick_steps: ‘No sugar added’ on the coconut water carton.
entry.science: Coconut water is the liquid inside green coconuts. It carries potassium, sodium, magnesium and phosphorus, in amounts that vary with the coconut’s maturity. There is no scientific proof it hydrates better than regular water. Some brands add sugar.

labels_decoded.meaning: Minerals such as potassium, sodium and magnesium.

entry.tier_note: Extension guidance backs the facts: coconut water carries the same minerals, and plain water hydrates as well.

entry.title: Energy drinks
entry.question: What should you buy instead of an energy drink?
entry.decision: Organic herb tea or mineral water, not energy drinks.
entry.why: Traditional guides list caffeine, added vitamins, citric acid and artificial sweeteners among drink ingredients to skip.
entry.short_answer: An energy drink stacks several things traditional guides skip in a drink: caffeine, added vitamins, citric acid, sweeteners and flavors. Organic herb tea without caffeine or natural flavors, or plain mineral water, is the swap.
entry.detail: The traditional shopping guide lists drinks containing caffeine, high fructose corn syrup, artificial sweeteners, sugar alcohols, stevia leaf extract, natural flavors, citric acid, ascorbic acid or added vitamins or minerals among drinks to avoid. Organic herb teas without natural flavors, citric acid and caffeine sit in the next tier, in moderation, with a caution that some herb teas can have drug-like effects. Plain mineral water in cans or glass bottles ranks first.

sources.name: Weston A. Price Foundation: Shopping guide categories

entry.title: Beer
entry.question: Which beer should you buy?
entry.why: Traditional guides list organic unpasteurized beer among acceptable drinks, below water and lacto-fermented drinks.
entry.short_answer: Organic unpasteurized beer sits in the traditional guide’s acceptable tier, with organic wine. Plain mineral water and lacto-fermented drinks rank above it. Drinks with natural flavors, sweeteners or added colors land on the avoid list.
entry.detail: The traditional shopping guide places organic unpasteurized beer and organic wine in its middle tier of drinks, alongside herb teas, in moderation. First place goes to organic lacto-fermented drinks in glass jars and plain mineral water in cans or glass bottles. Drinks containing high fructose corn syrup, agave, artificial sweeteners, natural flavors or citric acid are listed to avoid.

entry.title: Cookies
entry.question: Which cookies should you buy?
entry.decision: Sprouted whole-grain cookies, butter, natural sweetener.
entry.why: Traditional guides rank cookies of sprouted whole grain, traditional fats and organic natural sweeteners first.
entry.short_answer: The best cookies use soaked or sprouted whole-grain flour and butter or coconut oil. The sweetener is maple syrup or honey. Hydrogenated oils, refined sugar and corn syrup land on the avoid list.
entry.detail: The traditional shopping guide ranks cookies, bars and muffins made with organic natural sweeteners, soaked or sprouted whole-grain flour, soaked and dried nuts and seeds, and butter, coconut oil or other traditional fats first. Organic whole-grain flour with butter, palm oil or coconut oil is the next tier. It lists cookies made with non-organic grains, partially hydrogenated vegetable oils, or refined sweeteners such as sugar, high fructose corn syrup and agave to avoid, along with cookies containing natural flavors, coffee, chocolate, cocoa or cacao.

entry.title: Fruit snacks
entry.question: What should you buy instead of fruit snacks?
entry.decision: Dried fruit with only the fruit on the list.
entry.why: Fruit snacks lean on refined sweeteners, concentrated juice and dyes that traditional guides and CSPI flag.
entry.short_answer: Dried fruit with the fruit alone on the list is the swap. Fruit snacks are usually built on sugar, corn syrup or concentrated fruit juice. Traditional guides list all three to avoid, and some carry synthetic dyes.
entry.detail: The traditional shopping guide lists white sugar, corn syrup, high fructose corn syrup, brown rice syrup and concentrated fruit juices among sweeteners to avoid. CSPI names candy and gelatin desserts as common homes for synthetic dyes; Red 40 and Yellow 5 are the two most widely used, and Yellow 5 triggers hyperactivity in some children. Dyes are petroleum-based colors that do not occur in nature.

sources.name: Weston A. Price Foundation: Shopping guide categories

buying_tips: Dried fruit with only the fruit on the list.

entry.title: Candy
entry.question: Which candy should you buy?
entry.decision: Candy sweetened with honey or maple, no synthetic dyes.
entry.why: CSPI names candy as a main home for synthetic dyes, and traditional guides rank honey and maple over refined sugar.
entry.short_answer: Candy is where synthetic dyes concentrate: CSPI names candy for Red 3, Red 40, Yellow 5 and Blue 1. The better candy uses an organic natural sweetener such as raw honey, maple syrup or molasses. It carries no synthetic dye.
entry.detail: CSPI lists candy among the foods carrying synthetic dyes and says dyes are used almost solely in foods of low nutritional value. Red 3 caused thyroid tumors in rats; Red 40 is the most widely used dye; Yellow 5 triggers hyperactivity in some children. The traditional shopping guide ranks organic natural sweeteners such as molasses, maple syrup, coconut sugar and raw honey first, and lists white sugar, corn syrup, high fructose corn syrup, artificial sweeteners and sugar alcohols to avoid.
